# Opening

## 1 · Title and opening

Hello, thank you to everyone for being here. Today I am going to talk about my dissertation project and highlight some of what I found and then discuss my future directions with this work.

My dissertation explores the nature of Fourth Amendment protections and legal decision-making in post-Dobbs pregnancy-loss investigations.

It asks what happens when legal actors evaluate the evidence, the investigation, and the woman's conduct with the benefit of hindsight.

[Next slide → Post-Dobbs Landscape]{.cue}

# Pregnancy criminalization

## 2 · Post-Dobbs Landscape

When the Supreme Court eliminated the federal constitutional right to legal abortion access in Dobbs, the ability of state governments to regulate and criminalize pregnancy outcomes expanded overnight.

Today, 13 states enforce near-total abortion bans.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Anti-abortion advocates have focused their efforts on continuing to expand the enforcement tools available to criminalize suspected abortion-related activity—by crafting novel restrictions on pregnant women's access to telehealth services, FDA-approved medications, and even interstate travel.

[CLICK]{.cue}

As a result, nearly 30% of American women already live in a state where officials are newly empowered to investigate, arrest, and prosecute people for pregnancy-related behaviors and outcomes that were, until recently, protected before viability.

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

On paper, many state laws exempt the pregnant woman herself.

In practice, the exemption has not reliably protected women from investigation, arrest, or charges. Kentucky prosecutors reportedly charged a woman with fetal homicide despite the state's express exemption, and they later dropped that count.

[CLICK]{.cue}

[Next slide → Pregnancy Criminalization]{.cue}

## 3 · Pregnancy Criminalization

States prosecuted people for their own pregnancy outcomes long before Dobbs.

Pregnancy Justice identified 1,396 criminal cases from 2006 until the eve of Dobbs.

The post-Dobbs era has seen an expansion of these tactics. Pregnancy Justice identified at least 902 cases in the first three years after Dobbs.

My dissertation also asks who becomes a suspect when a pregnancy ends, and on what evidence.

[Next slide → Pregnancy-Loss Narratives]{.cue}

## 4 · Pregnancy-Loss Narratives

While most people assume that pregnancy will invariably end in a live, healthy birth—

[CLICK]{.cue}

unless the pregnant person chooses to intentionally end the pregnancy through abortion—

[CLICK]{.cue}

the reality is that this ignores the large percentage of pregnancies that end in miscarriage or stillbirth.

Quenby and colleagues set the risk of miscarriage at 15.3 percent of recognized pregnancies, and about one in every 170 births ends in a stillbirth after twenty weeks.

And this creates a problem for the enforcement of laws that criminalize abortion or other outcomes of pregnancy, because it makes it particularly difficult to identify which pregnancies are potential criminal activity.

[CLICK]{.cue}

While making this kind of clear distinction was always difficult for a variety of reasons related to the nature of pregnancy, it is particularly challenging today—as the technological innovation of medication abortion has further limited the outward or objective, easily quantifiable differences between voluntary and involuntary pregnancy loss.

[CLICK]{.cue}

So the only real key distinction between an "abortion" and a "miscarriage" is the pregnant person's state of mind at the time.

[CLICK]{.cue}

And while historically abortion prosecutions were often hampered by the difficulty of collecting admissible evidence that could be used to clearly establish the pregnant person's state of mind at the time, modern communication technology and the way that people live their lives digitally have effectively changed how and when these cases are likely to be investigated and pursued.

[Next slide → What Is an Abortion?]{.cue}

## 5 · What Is an Abortion?

What facts and information will people use to distinguish between lawful and unlawful forms of pregnancy loss?

What counts as an abortion depends on who is answering.

Before a state can punish someone for an illegal abortion, it needs a statute that defines the prohibited conduct. Legislators often define abortion in religious or political terms that differ from how clinicians use the word.

In clinical terms, a miscarriage is a spontaneous abortion. When a patient arrives for emergency care, no examination or blood test separates a self-managed abortion from a miscarriage.

Then there's how ordinary people make these judgments.

As Finkel explained, commonsense justice represents what ordinary people think is just and fair.

People think in narratives and prototypes.

Studies demonstrate that commonsense judgments also tend to operate through how people construct narratives or stories that integrate both objective facts and subjective motives.

Yet at the heart of the modern abortion debate is a lack of consensus about what an abortion even is, let alone how or when it ought to be criminally punished.

[Next slide → The Fourth Amendment]{.cue}

# Probable cause

## 6 · The Fourth Amendment

This widespread epistemological uncertainty creates an enforcement environment that is incompatible with the "fact on fact and clue on clue" methodology that suspicion-based review requires.

Unlike the substantive decisional privacy rights once secured by Roe v. Wade, the Fourth Amendment's protections are ultimately procedural.

The Fourth Amendment works by defining the methods government officials can use to enforce the law—irrespective of a particular law's substance.

First, it prohibits only unreasonable searches and seizures.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Second, it establishes that probable cause is a precondition to a valid warrant.

[Next slide → Probable cause]{.cue}

## 7 · Probable cause

In Illinois v. Gates, the Court described the magistrate's task as deciding whether—given all the circumstances in the affidavit—there is a fair probability that contraband or evidence of a crime will be found in a particular place.

No one, including the U.S. Supreme Court, can articulate precisely what the term probable cause means.

For the most part, this ambiguity is by design. Probable cause has no singular definition because courts need it to both embody multiple meanings and perform a variety of different functions. This plurality of purpose distinguishes probable cause from other legal burdens of proof that courts are more than happy to define.

Legal scholars have developed frameworks to bring analytical clarity to probable cause determinations.

Probable cause has to be found more than once in the same case.

If people assert their rights, courts evaluate the situation in hindsight.

[CLICK]{.cue}

The main studies examined two Fourth Amendment contexts—the review of a search warrant and the review of a warrantless arrest.

[Next slide → Probable cause and timing]{.cue}

## 8 · Probable cause and timing

However, in United States v. Di Re, the Court explained that "a search is not to be made legal by what it turns up. In law it is good or bad when it starts and does not change character from its success."

This means that legally, officials cannot rely on after-the-fact justifications for their actions, and courts cannot evaluate probable cause or reasonable suspicion in hindsight—based on what a search does or does not turn up.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Despite the continued rhetorical insistence that Fourth Amendment burdens of proof are forward-looking in nature, the Supreme Court's decisions have increasingly limited the number of settings that mandate any kind of meaningful before-the-fact review.

[CLICK]{.cue}

The Fourth Amendment's privacy-protecting function presumes that legal decision makers can reliably ignore irrelevant outcome information. Judges and other legal decision makers must disregard what they already know to have occurred and recapture the sense of uncertainty that would have existed beforehand.

[Next slide → Hindsight bias]{.cue}

# Hindsight

## 9 · Hindsight bias

The assumption that decision makers can evaluate evidence prospectively, judging what was reasonable at the time rather than being influenced by what happened after the fact, is central to Fourth Amendment doctrine but challenged by decades of psychological research.

Hindsight bias is the well-documented tendency of people with outcome knowledge to make inaccurate judgments about the past.

[Next slide → Components of hindsight bias]{.cue}

## 10 · Components of hindsight bias

Researchers have more formally conceptualized hindsight bias as comprising three distinct components—memory distortions, inevitability impressions, and foreseeability judgments.

[Next slide → Components of hindsight bias]{.cue}

## 11 · Components of hindsight bias

Each component is also thought to arise mainly from different processes, though no process belongs to one component alone.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Inevitability is concerned with people's objective understanding of the state of the world, so it is understood to be primarily driven by cognitive factors and sense-making processes.

Foreseeability is often driven by metacognitive processes, such as subjective experiences of process fluency.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Foreseeability points to overconfidence and myopia, while inevitability also points to myopia.

[Next slide → Retrospective sense-making]{.cue}

## 12 · Retrospective sense-making

[CLICK]{.cue}

Pezzo's sense-making model suggests that outcomes that provide high initial surprise invoke a process of trying to make sense of how the outcome could have happened.

If that process is successful, the outcome seems obvious and hindsight bias results. If it is not, hindsight bias can be reduced or even reversed.

[CLICK]{.cue}

People tend to focus on the antecedents that are consistent with the outcome—and to ignore or assign little value to those that are inconsistent with it.

The medical indistinguishability of abortion and miscarriage means that the preliminary evidence often supports multiple interpretations—which are the conditions under which the sense-making model predicts robust outcome effects.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Sometimes an event may appear inevitable, yet still unpredictable, in hindsight.

[Next slide → Probable cause and hindsight]{.cue}

## 13 · Probable cause and hindsight

Both of these hindsight components are likely used in the probable cause analysis.

[CLICK]{.cue}

But the legal standard is not simply a probabilistic judgment—it also contains a component of reasonableness, which also makes the outcome bias relevant.

Whereas hindsight bias concerns whether people think an outcome was predictable, outcome bias concerns whether people think a decision was good or bad based on how it turned out.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Kneer and Skoczeń proposed that outcome knowledge leads to exaggerated impressions of the probability of harm and then, in turn, to greater attributions of negligence and blame.

These moral judgments are relevant to the probable cause inquiry—because they likely influence perceptions of culpability and of reasonable belief that someone committed a crime, as opposed to a lawful tragedy.

[Next slide → Program of Research]{.cue}

# The studies

## 14 · Program of Research

Yet limited empirical research has examined whether the behavioral and moral assumptions underlying these interlocking legal frameworks actually reflect how people make decisions in this context.

Across four studies—two pilots, with 81 and 309 people, and two main studies, with 398 and 320—I examined three questions:

- what people regarded as evidence of a pregnancy-related crime, and when they considered it sufficient for a search or arrest
- how abortion and gender attitudes related to these judgments
- whether outcome knowledge changed evaluations of the earlier evidence, the detective's decision, and the woman's conduct

[Next slide → Pilot 1: Narrative content]{.cue}

## 15 · Pilot 1: Narrative content

In Pilot Study 1, I examined the narrative prototypes people hold for four abortion-related crimes.

Results indicated that people's narratives distinguished the four crime categories most sharply on the features that describe what the defendant did.

[Next slide → Pilot 2: Search scenarios]{.cue}

## 16 · Pilot 2: Search scenarios

For Pilot Study 2, I wrote three search warrant affidavits informed by the Pilot Study 1 narratives—a self-managed abortion, a non-criminal miscarriage, and a criminal miscarriage.

In Pilot Study 2 and both main studies, people knew about the pregnancy loss from the start.

What I varied was the information they learned after the police acted.

The results were to show which of three scenarios produced the strongest outcome-knowledge effect on judgments of likelihood, foreseeability, and the subjective probability of guilt.

I chose the non-criminal miscarriage scenario for Study 1.

That scenario had the numerically largest increases in guilt and self-managed-abortion likelihood after the expected incriminating evidence—but the smallest change in foreseeability.

[Next slide → Study 1: Search-warrant evaluations]{.cue}

# Study 1

## 17 · Study 1: Search-warrant evaluations

In Study 1, 398 people evaluated the evidence supporting a single search warrant.

The design crossed two factors. Search outcome information had three levels: no information, self-managed-abortion evidence, which was the expected incriminating evidence, and financial evidence, which was the unexpected incriminating evidence. Legal context had two: illegal abortion and improper disposal of human remains.

People in the foresight condition evaluated the search warrant affidavit without learning what the search found. People in the search outcome conditions learned that the search had uncovered expected or unexpected incriminating evidence—and were instructed to disregard that information when assessing the search.

[Next slide → Study 1: Materials & Procedure]{.cue}

## 18 · Study 1: Materials & Procedure

Following the search scenario, they first made the probable cause ruling and then answered the remaining case judgments.

[Next slide → Study 1: Outcome likelihood]{.cue}

## 19 · Study 1: Outcome likelihood

To measure perceptions of the inevitability of each possible search outcome, people rated the likelihood that the search would reveal each one—from 0 to 100.

[CLICK]{.cue}

As predicted, people who learned that the search found self-managed-abortion evidence rated pregnancy-related evidence as more likely to be found than people in the foresight condition—54.4 versus 41.8.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Similarly, people who learned that it found financial evidence rated financial-crime evidence as more likely—45 versus 17.4.

[Next slide → Study 1: Retrospective sense-making]{.cue}

## 20 · Study 1: Retrospective sense-making

I hypothesized that part of the effect of outcome information on the likelihood of pregnancy-related evidence would go through people's reinterpretation of the evidence—raising it after self-managed-abortion evidence, and lowering it after financial evidence, compared with the foresight condition.

I measured evidence reinterpretation with relative relevance—the mean rating of the facts that fit a self-managed abortion, minus the mean rating of the other facts.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Consistent with the hypothesis, self-managed-abortion evidence raised relative relevance in both legal contexts—1.08 for illegal abortion, 1.54 for improper disposal.

Higher relative relevance was associated with a higher likelihood of pregnancy-related evidence.

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

The indirect effect of self-managed-abortion evidence on likelihood through relative relevance was therefore positive in both legal contexts:

- illegal abortion—2.48, 95% interval from 0.54 to 5.06
- improper disposal—3.54, from 1.55 to 6.07

Financial evidence, however, did not significantly change relative relevance in either legal context—and neither indirect effect differed from zero.

[Next slide → Study 1: Foreseeability]{.cue}

## 21 · Study 1: Foreseeability

Hindsight bias could affect the probable cause analysis by distorting either perceptions of the outcome's inevitability or foreseeability.

[CLICK]{.cue}

People who learned that the search found financial evidence rated the outcome as less foreseeable than people who learned that it found self-managed-abortion evidence—by 0.56 points in both legal contexts.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Compared with no outcome information, financial evidence lowered foreseeability only in the improper disposal context.

[Next slide → Study 1: Decision quality]{.cue}

## 22 · Study 1: Decision quality

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

In both legal contexts, pregnancy-evidence likelihood and foreseeability were each significantly and positively associated with the rated quality of the detective's decision.

[CLICK]{.cue}

This has implications for how these different hindsight components might affect real-world decisions, because in exclusionary rule contexts judges are asked not only to consider probable cause, but to consider it from the perspective of the reasonable officer.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Probable cause depends on what an objectively reasonable officer could have anticipated regarding the search outcome at the time.

[Next slide → Study 1: Probable-cause rulings]{.cue}

## 23 · Study 1: Probable-cause rulings

Moreover, I also found that—as hypothesized—people were more likely to find probable cause after learning that the search uncovered self-managed-abortion evidence. Averaged over the two legal contexts, the predicted probability was 64 percent—versus 41 percent in the foresight condition.

That difference was consistent with people reinterpreting the supporting evidence in a way that made the search appear more justified—after being exposed to information about what was ultimately found in the search.

However, incriminating evidence found during a search cannot supply probable cause that was missing before it began.

[Next slide → Study 1: Attitudes and moral judgments]{.cue}

## 24 · Study 1: Attitudes and moral judgments

People's attitudes toward gender roles and abortion were also associated with how harshly they judged the conduct of women suspected of pregnancy-related crimes.

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

Consistent with the exploratory predictions, people higher in hostile sexism and in benevolent sexism endorsed harsher punishment of the suspect—the total indirect associations were 0.33 for hostile sexism and 0.18 for benevolent sexism.

However, these associations did not clearly extend to susceptibility to hindsight and outcome bias.

[Next slide → Study 2: False-arrest claim]{.cue}

# Study 2

## 25 · Study 2: False-arrest claim

In Study 2, 320 people acted as jurors in a section 1983 case—a false-arrest claim brought by a woman who had been arrested for reckless feticide after a pregnancy loss at home.

The prosecutor had declined the criminal case—concluding that the reckless-feticide statute was not intended to apply to a woman's conduct concerning her own pregnancy.

People in the no-information condition received no outcome information. People in the outcome conditions learned that the post-arrest investigation had determined that the loss was a self-managed abortion—or a non-criminal miscarriage—and were instructed to disregard that information when deciding whether the detective had probable cause.

I also varied the woman's circumstances and reported conduct—to present either a stereotypical or a non-stereotypical pre-arrest record.

[Next slide → Study 2: Materials & Procedure]{.cue}

## 26 · Study 2: Materials & Procedure

All participants then received pattern jury instructions, which included an explicit instruction to ignore any information learned after the arrest when deciding whether the detective had probable cause.

[Next slide → Study 2: Outcome likelihood]{.cue}

## 27 · Study 2: Outcome likelihood

[CLICK]{.cue}

People given no outcome information judged miscarriage less likely when the evidence available before the arrest fit a self-managed abortion narrative than when it did not—39.2 versus 57.7.

[CLICK]{.cue}

As in Study 1, learning an incriminating outcome changed people's likelihood judgments—even though they were asked to judge only from what was known at the time of the arrest.

Self-managed abortion information lowered the rated likelihood of miscarriage after both records:

- stereotypical record—27.2 versus 39.2
- non-stereotypical record—31.3 versus 57.7, although it had been predicted to raise it after that record

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

Non-criminal miscarriage information did not significantly change it after either record.

In the primary sample—contrary to the central stereotypicality prediction—the effects of outcome information on likelihood judgments did not differ significantly between the two records.

[Next slide → Study 2: Probable-cause rulings]{.cue}

## 28 · Study 2: Probable-cause rulings

I hypothesized that people would be more likely to find probable cause:

- after self-managed abortion information than in the no-information condition
- and—accounting for retrospective likelihood and perceived foreseeability—after self-managed abortion information than after non-criminal miscarriage information

Contrary to the hypotheses, averaged over the two records, neither difference was significant. The predicted probabilities, by record:

- stereotypical record—28 percent with no information, 50 after self-managed abortion information, 33 after non-criminal miscarriage information
- non-stereotypical record—35, 38, and 29 percent

[Next slide → Study 2: Moral judgments]{.cue}

## 29 · Study 2: Moral judgments

[CLICK]{.cue}

As predicted, people given self-managed abortion information blamed the plaintiff more than people given non-criminal miscarriage information—4.42 versus 3.19, on a 7-point scale.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Contrary to the hypothesis, they did not endorse significantly harsher punishment—2.72 versus 2.42.

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

However, they judged her more reckless—5.25 versus 3.69—and more negligent—5.43 versus 3.74—than people given non-criminal miscarriage information.

[Next slide → Main Findings]{.cue}

# Discussion

## 30 · Main Findings

[CLICK]{.cue}

In Study 1, self-managed abortion evidence did increase probable cause findings.

In Study 2, however, the primary adjusted comparison with no outcome information did not establish more probable cause findings.

Knowing how the investigation turned out influenced people's likelihood judgments in Study 1 and Study 2, despite instructions to evaluate only the evidence available beforehand.

[CLICK]{.cue}

In Study 1, learning of self-managed abortion evidence also improved evaluations of the warrant decision relative to no outcome information.

In Study 2, contrary to the predicted outcome bias, neither kind of outcome information significantly changed evaluations of the detective or his decision to arrest.

[CLICK]{.cue}

In Study 1, people who learned that the search found self-managed-abortion evidence also blamed the suspect more than people in the foresight condition.

In Study 2, people given self-managed abortion information blamed the plaintiff more than people given non-criminal miscarriage information.

The Study 1 findings raise the concern that the commonsense assessment the law requires may depend partly on knowledge of what a search found.

[Next slide → Limitations and Future Directions]{.cue}

## 31 · Limitations and Future Directions

The use of lay participants limits what the present studies can establish about judicial decision-making.

[CLICK]{.cue}

Comparing judges and lay observers in a larger study—with tasks that more closely resemble actual proceedings—would help clarify whether judges are less susceptible to these hindsight effects.

[CLICK]{.cue}

The use of a single type of fact pattern in each main study also limits generalization across other circumstances, search findings, and stages of pregnancy.

The studies did not isolate evidence strength.

In Study 2, many people did not correctly identify the outcome information in the case file, and several conclusions about likelihood judgments, punishment, and evaluations of the detective changed in the sensitivity sample.

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

I measured evidence relevance rather than manipulating people's interpretation of it, and people in the main studies rated relevance after making their probable cause ruling.

I adopted relative relevance after examining the registered results.

The indirect effects also cannot establish that the sense-making process produced the bias.

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

The future of efforts to restrict and police abortion seems to be focused on politically palatable approaches: limiting access to medication abortion, and finding ways to sell it as particularly dangerous and grotesque.

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

[CLICK]{.cue}

Anti-abortion advocates have also tried to turn the Comstock Act, an 1873 postal obscenity law, into a nationwide abortion ban that would stop the mailing of abortion pills.

That would make the future of abortion criminalization look more like the war on drugs, and the first criminalization campaign, than the types of prosecutions that were more common in the period before Roe.

These efforts present a lot of uncertainty about the future.

These findings provide empirical evidence about how people interpret a pregnancy loss—and how they judge whether the surrounding facts justify government intrusion.

Overall, more research on the intersection of abortion criminalization and Fourth Amendment issues is needed.

And so my plan at this point is to spend the spring publishing this work and other projects to continue to apply for academic jobs that begin next year.
